title: Multiclass Classification
subtitle: Topic: Multiclass Classification · Subject: Supervised Machine Learning. Three beginner, two medium and two advanced questions with seven original SVG lessons, balanced explanatory choices and beginner-first explanations.
hero:
MULTICLASS CLASSIFICATION · VISUAL STUDY

Choose one class from three or more possibilities

Multiclass classification trains on one correct label per example. Models can produce a score for each class, turn those scores into a probability distribution, and choose the highest-scoring class while still tracking errors for every category.

questions.tag: Beginner · Exactly one of several classes
questions.stem: What is Multiclass Classification in supervised machine learning, and how is it different from binary and multi-label classification?
options: Multiclass classification predicts any number of independent labels for one example, while binary classification predicts exactly one of three or more labels. Multi-label classification instead always requires exactly two possible categories.

Multiclass classification uses labeled examples to predict exactly one class among three or more mutually exclusive classes. Binary classification offers two choices; multi-label classification permits several classes to be true simultaneously.

Multiclass classification predicts a continuous numerical outcome that is divided into categories after training. Unlike binary learning, it needs no class labels because the model discovers its groups from input similarity.

Multiclass classification trains a separate regression target for every class and permits all classes to be selected. Binary classification and multi-label classification both require a single mutually exclusive class per example.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Multiclass classification is supervised learning where each example belongs to exactly one of three or more classes. A fruit photo might be labeled apple, banana, or pear, but not several of them at once. Binary classification has only two mutually exclusive choices. Multi-label classification is different because a photo could receive several independent tags, such as dog and tree. These distinctions determine how targets and outputs should be represented. The model learns from labeled examples and predicts the class for new cases.

questions.tag: Beginner · Logits, softmax and choosing a class
questions.stem: How does a Multiclass Classification model convert raw class scores into probabilities, and what does argmax select from a three-class prediction?
options: Softmax clips every score separately between zero and one without considering other classes. Argmax then selects the class with the lowest resulting value, making the predicted label independent of score ordering.
Softmax applies a separate sigmoid to every class score, so the outputs can sum to more than one. Argmax chooses every class whose probability exceeds the default threshold of 0.5.
Softmax subtracts the smallest class score from every score and divides by the total score sum. Argmax uses the average probability to choose the class nearest the mean, not the most likely class.

Softmax exponentiates and normalizes scores into probabilities that sum to one. For logits [2,1,0], probabilities are approximately [0.665,0.245,0.090], and argmax chooses the first class with the largest score.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A multiclass model may produce one unbounded score, called a logit, for each class. Softmax converts logits into nonnegative probabilities that sum to one by exponentiating and normalizing them together. For scores [2,1,0], the probabilities are about [0.665,0.245,0.090]. Argmax selects the class with the highest value, here the first class. For example, an animal-image classifier might favor cat over dog and bird. The full probability vector still contains useful uncertainty information that the hard label discards.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 02 · MULTICLASS CLASSIFICATION

With logits [2,1,0], softmax gives approximately [0.665,0.245,0.090]. They sum to one, and argmax selects cat as the predicted class.

questions.stem: Why is categorical cross-entropy commonly used for Multiclass Classification, and how are one-hot and integer class-index targets related?
options: Categorical cross-entropy penalizes low probability assigned to the true class. A dog target may be represented as one-hot [0,1,0] or integer index 1; with p_dog=0.70, loss is about 0.357.

Categorical cross-entropy penalizes only the number of wrong class predictions, not their probabilities. One-hot targets select the predicted class, while integer indices measure the numerical distance between category identifiers.

Categorical cross-entropy requires each of the three classes to be independently true or false, so one-hot labels are invalid. Integer indices must first be converted to three unrelated binary classification problems.

Categorical cross-entropy minimizes the sum of predicted class scores before normalization. One-hot targets and integer indices represent different learning tasks even when both indicate exactly the same true class.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Categorical cross-entropy compares a multiclass probability distribution with the true class. When the target is one-hot, the loss equals the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to the correct class. A dog label can be encoded as [0,1,0] or, with a compatible sparse-loss API, integer class index 1. If the model assigns dog probability 0.70, the loss is −ln(0.70)≈0.357. For raw logits, use a loss implementation that includes stable log-softmax rather than applying softmax twice.

questions.stem: How should a three-by-three confusion matrix be interpreted for Multiclass Classification, and what accuracy results from diagonal counts 18, 8, and 6 out of 40 cases?
options: A three-class confusion matrix has one row per predicted class and no actual-class axis. Its accuracy is the largest diagonal count divided by all cases, giving 18/40=45% in this example.

Every off-diagonal cell represents a correct alternative prediction, so overall accuracy includes all 40 cases. The diagonal instead measures class imbalance and cannot be used to calculate classification accuracy.
With actual labels on rows and predicted labels on columns, diagonal cells are correct predictions. Here 18+8+6=32 of 40 are correct, giving 80% accuracy; off-diagonal cells show class confusions.
Accuracy is the unweighted average of the three diagonal counts, divided by the number of classes rather than examples. The values 18, 8, and 6 therefore imply 32/3, or 10.7% accuracy.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A multiclass confusion matrix compares every true class with every predicted class. Here rows are actual cat, dog, and bird, while columns are predicted labels. The diagonal counts correct predictions: 18 cats, 8 dogs, and 6 birds, totaling 32 correct out of 40. Accuracy is therefore 80%. The other eight cells count wrong classifications. For example, three true dogs were predicted as cats. The matrix shows which categories are confused, which overall accuracy alone cannot reveal.

Rows show true cat, dog and bird; columns show predicted labels. The diagonal counts 18+8+6=32 correct out of 40, so overall accuracy is 80%.

questions.stem: How can Multiclass Classification be implemented in scikit-learn with an honest train/test split, and how should accuracy and macro F1 be evaluated?
options: Fit StandardScaler on every example before splitting to preserve global statistics, then train LogisticRegression only on training labels. Compute macro F1 from the training set while reporting test accuracy as a separate score.

Create a stratified train/test split, fit StandardScaler and multiclass LogisticRegression inside a training pipeline, then predict held-out labels. Compute confusion matrix, accuracy, and macro F1 without fitting preprocessing on test examples.

Train LogisticRegression independently for every test class by repeatedly fitting the test subset. Combine those test models and compute accuracy after selecting whichever model produces the highest class-specific F1 score.

Fit the classifier on the entire dataset but hold back labels until evaluation, allowing the scaler to see all test features. Macro F1 then measures the percentage of all individually correct predictions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: First split labeled data, preferably stratifying to retain class proportions. A Pipeline fits StandardScaler on training features and trains LogisticRegression on the transformed data. It uses the learned scaler to process held-out features without fitting again. The example uses 180 training and 60 test cases for three classes. Its test confusion matrix is [[30,0,0],[0,18,0],[0,3,9]], with 95.0% accuracy and about 92.7% macro F1. Macro F1 is the mean of the class-specific F1 scores, not simply accuracy.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 05 · MULTICLASS CLASSIFICATION
scikit-learn · Three-class LogisticRegression 15 lines
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, f1_score, accuracy_score
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=240, n_features=6, n_informative=4,
    n_redundant=0, n_classes=3, n_clusters_per_class=1,
    weights=[.5,.3,.2], class_sep=1.15, random_state=12)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25,
    stratify=y, random_state=11)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=500))
pred = model.fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)
print(confusion_matrix(yte, pred).tolist())
print(round(accuracy_score(yte,pred),3), round(f1_score(yte,pred,average=""macro""),3))

The 15-line scikit-learn example fits StandardScaler only on 180 training samples and evaluates on 60 held-out cases. It scores 95.0% accuracy and 92.7% macro F1.

questions.stem: What is the difference between macro, micro, and weighted F1 in Multiclass Classification, especially when some classes are much more common than others?
options: Macro F1 weights classes by their training frequency, while weighted F1 treats all classes equally. Micro F1 reports the F1 score of the rarest class only, so it is independent of common-class performance.

Macro, micro, and weighted F1 always give identical scores for any mutually exclusive multiclass task, regardless of class imbalance. The averaging choices only have a meaningful difference for binary classification.

Macro F1 sums all predictions before calculating one global score, while micro F1 averages each class equally. Weighted F1 multiplies each class score by its number of predicted positives rather than true support.
Macro F1 averages class F1 scores equally; weighted F1 uses each class's true support; micro F1 pools prediction counts globally. On the illustrated 40 cases they are about 78.4%, 79.7%, and 80.0%.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To evaluate a multiclass model, calculate an F1 score for each class. Macro F1 averages these scores equally, making performance on rare classes visible. Weighted F1 averages using the number of true examples in each class, while micro F1 pools prediction counts. In single-label multiclass classification, micro F1 equals accuracy. For the 40-case confusion matrix, macro F1 is about 78.4%, weighted F1 about 79.7%, and micro F1 80.0%. These differences matter when class frequencies are unequal.

QUESTION 06 · MULTICLASS CLASSIFICATION

On the 40-case matrix, class F1s are 85.7%, 69.6%, and 80.0%. Macro F1 is 78.4%, micro F1 is 80.0%, and support-weighted F1 is 79.7%.

questions.tag: Advanced · Honest multiclass evaluation and model strategy
questions.stem: How should Multiclass Classification handle class imbalance, model selection, data leakage, and monitoring when deployed on changing real-world examples?
options: Fit the model and preprocessing on training data, compare models and per-class metrics on validation data, and reserve test data for final evaluation. Monitor rare-class errors and drift; one-vs-rest is optional, not mandatory.

Fit preprocessing across training and test sets to stabilize class statistics, then choose the winning model by repeated test F1 checks. Once test performance is high, rare-class monitoring is unnecessary after deployment.

Use only overall accuracy for selecting multiclass models because it weights every class equally, regardless of support. An independent test set is optional as long as softmax probabilities always sum exactly to one.

Replace the multiclass model with separate binary classifiers for each class in every case, since all neural networks require one-vs-rest. Refit threshold choices on test labels whenever class frequencies change.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Multiclass systems need evaluation beyond a single accuracy number. Fit preprocessing and model parameters only using training data, choose models and check per-class performance with validation data, and preserve an untouched test set for final estimates. Stratification can help when classes are uneven, while group or time splits may be necessary to prevent leakage. Native multiclass models are available; one-vs-rest is an optional strategy, not a universal requirement. After deployment, monitor rare-class failures, changing class frequencies, and probability calibration.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 07 · MULTICLASS CLASSIFICATION

Use training data for fitting; validation for model selection and calibration checks; untouched test data for final scores. Track per-class errors, imbalance, and changing classes after deployment.
